prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned prose that turns memory, the body and dream into large metaphysical architectures.

statement.case_for: Cărtărescu remains my first choice on the criterion I find hardest to meet: a voice I hear in this writer's work and nowhere else. Blinding and Solenoid, as publicly described, build long, architecturally complex books in which memory, the body and dream become a sustained metaphysical project. The formal ambition is matched by an imaginative depth that does not read as borrowed from any single tradition. The prose draws on the European fantastic and on modernist encyclopedism, but it is not derivative of them. He began as a poet, and the lyrical intensity of the prose is part of the achievement. The career spans several decades, and the major novels appear to extend rather than repeat the early project. That counts toward the maturity and sustained quality the will's framework asks for. The case is a literary one: it rests on voice, form and imaginative reach, not on reputation, nationality or the visibility of the language.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that I would be judging very stylised Romanian prose through translation, and the density and musicality that make the case may not carry over. I cannot independently verify the whole corpus. My coverage of his poetry and earlier work is thinner than my coverage of the large novels. There is also a substantive worry about the late, very large books. Scale and self-referentiality may blur the distinctness of individual volumes. Metaphysical ambition could outrun emotional and moral range. If the committee concluded that the intensity does not hold across the full corpus, the case would weaken materially.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first as the strongest case on formal and linguistic achievement. He argues that the poetry remade Arabic poetic language through myth and fragmentation, and that the essays extend this into critical thought. He also flags that translation conveys Arabic prosody only partially.
responses.response: I take the formal and linguistic claim seriously. I placed Adonis third because the achievement is large, and I agree it is mature and not a question of timing. Where I qualify it is the caveat Olsson himself raises. Much of the case rests on prosody and diction that none of us can judge directly in translation, and part of the significance is historical and critical influence, which must be separated from the quality of individual poems. Cărtărescu's case is also carried partly through translation, so I do not claim the translation problem favours one side. I would ask what, in the poems themselves, is demonstrably distinct from the importance of the renewal. Adonis stays my first alternative, and I would not oppose him if the committee can establish that.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first on distinctiveness of voice and sustained inventive reach. He notes that the late novels extend rather than repeat the earlier project. He also raises whether the metaphysical scale is matched by emotional and moral range.
responses.response: I agree on voice and on the extension of the project, and I would not rest the case on scale alone. His last question is the one I take as the real test, and I share it. My answer is provisional. The strongest passages I know of in the work are the ones where the body and childhood memory anchor the vision, which suggests the human dimension is not absent. But I cannot say that holds across the late volumes. If it does not, the case narrows to virtuosity of design, and I would then weigh Adonis or Michon more heavily.

responses.point: Swärd ranks Adonis first and Can Xue second. She values Can Xue's formally uncompromising dream fiction, but asks whether the oeuvre has the range the will implies or is one strong method repeated. She also notes Cărtărescu's durability across very large volumes is untested.
responses.response: The question about Can Xue is fair, and it is why I ranked her seventh. I had the same doubt about repetition of a signature mode. I do not think the same objection applies in the same way to Cărtărescu, whose project has moved through poetry, the Blinding cycle and Solenoid at different scales. I accept her point that durability across the long volumes remains to be tested, and I would not claim it is settled. Her uncertainty about whether Can Xue's method deepens or merely persists is one I cannot resolve either, because I depend on a partial selection in translation.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson first for a distinctive voice that fuses classical scholarship, lyric, narrative and book-object form, with a consistent method over decades. She places Cărtărescu third and names excess and repetition within the largest works as a possible weakness.
responses.response: I accept the worry about excess and repetition in the largest works. It is close to my own concern about self-referentiality in the late books. On Carson, I recognise the formal invention. But I did not rank her in my opening, because I am unsure how much of the achievement lies in hybrid and book-object forms that translation cannot carry, and how much in the breadth of the oeuvre beyond a few well-known works. If Palm can say which works demonstrate sustained quality across the corpus, I would reconsider how I weigh her.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's density and musicality survives translation from Romanian, and whether quality holds across the full corpus, including the poetry and early work, which I have not independently verified.
Whether the late, very large novels maintain moral and emotional range or mainly extend structural ambition.
How to separate historical and critical influence from the quality of individual poems in the case for Adonis, given that Arabic prosody is not directly accessible to me.
Whether Can Xue's method deepens over a large output or repeats, which cannot be judged from the partial translated selection available to me.
The breadth of Michon's compact oeuvre relative to the whole-life standard, and my thinner knowledge of his later works.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It documents her as a novelist and critic, but her own literary practice is context and not evidence of preference for any candidate. It lists no documented personal or professional tie to Mircea Cărtărescu or the other shortlisted writers.
